newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Ogoni activists say Nigeria increasingly brutal.
newsitem.headline: Ogoni activists say Nigeria increasingly brutal.

text.p: A human rights group led by Nigerian activist Ken Saro-Wiwa until his execution a year ago said on Thursday that Nigeria's military rulers were increasingly brutal in stamping down on the opposition.

The Movement for the Survival of Ogoni People (MOSOP) also accused oil company Shell of conniving with the government of General Sani Abacha and of being the main source of anguish for the people of Nigeria's oil-rich Ogoniland.
"The Ogoni people hold Shell primarily responsible for our anguish," MOSOP said in a statement released in South Africa.

"It is our firm belief that in so far as Shell, exhibiting all the attributes of a quasi-state entity in Nigeria, is not held accountable by the international community for the consequences of its action, the much desired change towards the restoration of democracy, respect for human rights and environmental justice in Nigeria will remain elusive," it said.
Ogoniland is troubled by efforts to achieve self- determination for the 500,000-strong community which MOSOP championed under the leadership of Saro-Wiwa, an author.
Nigeria caused international outrage on November 10 last year when Saro-Wiwa and eight others were hanged for the murder of four pro-government Ogoni chiefs.

The nine activists had been tried under a military decree condemned worldwide as unfair. Nigeria was suspended from the Commonwealth grouping largely Britrain and its former colonies. Other Western states followed with token sanctions.
MOSOP said one year of mourning for the activists had ended with little progress towards democracy.

"Many had hoped that the global condemnation of the executions and the token sanctions put in place against the Nigerian regime would induce some relaxation of the repression in Ogoni in particular and the country in general," it said.
"That that hope is totally misplaced is manifest in the increased militarisation and repression unrivalled in any period of our time."

The group said it was prepared for negotiations on Nigeria's problems in an atmosphere of freedom, but there was currently no freedom of movement or assembly in Ogoni and MOSOP supporters were unable to meet.
In the past year many people in the international community had sacrificed their principles on the "altar of oil politics".
"Many world leaders who voiced disgust soon after the executions appear to have beaten a retreat," it added.

Police in the oil-producing area of southeastern Nigeria have banned demonstrations to mark the first anniversary on Sunday of the hanging of the activists. MOSOP leaders inside Nigeria said there would be no mass rallies, in an effort to avoid clashes with the authorities.
South Africa emerged as the champion of sanctions on Nigeria after the hangings and the release of the MOSOP statement there appeared to be in recognition of that role.
